caretakers who came before us.

reflect on the importance of September 30th, Orange Shirt Day and the National Day for
truth and reconciliation. This day serves as a solemn reminder of the enduring legacy
of the residential school system and the harm it inflicted on Indigenous children, families
and communities across Canada. The impacts are not confined to the past. They continue
to echo through current generations. This year, the heartbreaking discovery of 41 additional
unmarked graves at the Shishalsh residential school is a stark reminder that the journey
towards truth and healing is far from complete.
The trauma inflicted by residential schools and the broader legacy of colonialism is something
we all must confront.
We must acknowledge the deep cultural harm imposed on First Nations, Inuit and Métis
peoples.
We need to understand and show empathy and empathy must guide us as we learn Canada's
true history.
On this day, we urge every resident of Kitchener to honour the survivors and the children who
never returned home.
Tomorrow is a day for solemn remembrance and a reaffirmation of our collective commitment
to listening, understanding and supporting Indigenous communities.
The members of Kitchener Council and our City staff are committed to continuing to learn
and understand the history and current reality of Indigenous peoples.
We're committed to tackling systemic anti-Indigenous racism and ensuring these vital conversations
and actions remain central in our governance and community life.
Each of us has a role to play in this crucial work, such as attending Indigenous-led events,
wearing an orange shirt, or engaging in personal reflection and education.
By listening to the stories and experiences of Indigenous peoples, we foster a community
grounded in respect and solidarity.
To help centre and create space for deeper reflection on the National Day of Truth and
Reconciliation this year, the City collaborated with Jack Spicer-Foller, a local Indigenous
artist, youth artist, to create a powerful visual representation of healing and connection.
You can see that visual representation on the screen above me.
The artwork, titled Journey Home, will be featured in publications and on digital platforms
in 2025 and is a powerful reminder of the strength, resilience and realities that continue
to shape our community.
Let us come together in unity to recognize the resilience and invaluable contributions
of Indigenous peoples to both Kitchener and our broader world. Today, tomorrow, and every
day we pledge to walk the path of truth and reconciliation with sincerity and hope, aspiring
to build a future that embraces equity and justice for all.
